MegaMan+attack aligned (both on black): REAL f58 vs RUST f139, best-shift residual ~54%. Attack shape/pose/scale match; residual is the ORB TRAVEL PHASE (real orb at muzzle vs rust orb further out) + HP '100' text.

MegaMan+attack scale match (both on black): REAL f57 vs RUST f132 — same firing pose, green cannon barrel, orb at muzzle. The 66x40 vs 46x38 bbox diff is because the real's orb touches the barrel; shapes match closely.
Diagnosis: the MegaMan blue-body silhouette MATCHES (same shape real vs rust). The per-frame residual is the barrel/orb position + pose/timing, not a wrong navi or projectile.
Barrel-anchor matched (real f51 vs rust f132): both green compact barrel at the arm. Residual: exact sprite pixels/colors + HP text, not structure.

DIFFMASK after col-2 fix: residual 10%->6.93%, both MegaMan aligned at (0,0). Background solid green (identical). Red = MegaMan sprite pixels + Mettaur/HP/HUD extra elements.

DIFFMASK real f58 vs rust f137 (cannon big-orb frame, enemy deleted, banner blanked): 0/38400 differing. Every frame c0-c35 of the Cannon is now 0 px different within x<140 (c6 = banner re-upload artifact). Fixes: full 13-frame barrel anim 0 incl. discharge, silhouette palette, 0x1e pose + anim 15 recovery, OAM part order, barrel over navi, hidden shot, no player HP object.

SWORD matched: tools/chip_compare.py 47 demo-sword -> 0 px on every frame c0-c39 (c6 = banner artifact). Real objects: sprite_82EFE48 anim 0 (sword, from the slash state's first frame), sprite_830F144 anim 2 (arc at front panel -16, over the sword, spawned on pose frame 10). Cannon re-checked: still 0.

AIRSHOT matched: tools/chip_compare.py 04 demo-airshot -> 0 px on every frame (c6 = banner artifact). Arm object sprite_83138C4 anim 0 at (+18,-24) for the 21-frame pose (anim 9); the gust is its frames 1-4; instant one-panel hit on frame 6.

MINIBOMB matched (x<140 window; landing at ~x180 not yet compared): tools/chip_compare.py 36 demo-minibomb -> 0 px on every frame c0-c49 (c6 = banner artifact). Held bomb sprite_82F569C anim 0 on the origin until the throw (pose frame 10), thrown bomb anim 1 with the game's 16.16 physics (2.9 px/f, +2.02 up, -0.156 gravity, 40 frames), shadow part kept on the ground, Y and Z floored separately; animation 6 held 42 frames.

MINIBOMB landing matched too: --xmax 240 -> 0 px c42-c74 (the blast sprite_8399578 anim 0 at the landing panel, 22 frames, sound 0x70; the earlier full-width residue is the real ROM's dissolving Mettaur remnant).

VULCAN1 matched: tools/chip_compare.py 05 demo-vulcan -> 0 px on every frame c0-c49 (c6 = banner artifact). Arm gun sprite_83195F0 at (+23,-25): anim 0 (cream flash, own, held) in the first state, anim 1 (the 5-frame firing loop with muzzle flashes) from the firing state's first frame, anim 2 held in the last; navi anim 10 x2, anim 13 x20, anim 10 x13; the three shots are invisible in flight.

HICANNON matched: tools/chip_compare.py 02 demo-hicannon -> 0 px on every frame. The real ROM's hand validation swaps unowned chips for the bug chip 0x185 (encryption_testPack_8006e84: library byte ^ 0x81 must equal its copy); the comparer now fakes the library entry. HiCannon = the Cannon barrel with palette 1 (byte_80B8BD4 row 1).
LONGSWRD matched: tools/chip_compare.py 49 demo-longswrd -> 0 px on every frame (sword object + arc animation 1, two panels ahead), once the library poke lets the real ROM keep it in the hand.
RECOV30 matched: tools/chip_compare.py 9b demo-recov30 --rust-start 123 -> 0 px on every frame (same heal effect as Recov10).

BARRIER matched: tools/chip_compare.py b2 demo-barrier --frames 190 --rust-start 123 -> 0 px on every frame (c18/c159 = banner artifact). Presentation 77 frames (measured), then the bubble sprite_832F8C8 anim 0 (dot + 3 bubble frames, x4, looping; its lighter palettes 1/2 via OAM palette offsets) 2 px forward of the origin, drawn above the navi's shadow and under its body, while the barrier has HP.

INVISIBL matched: tools/chip_compare.py b1 demo-invisibl --frames 190 --rust-start 123 -> 0 px on every frame. Presentation 128 frames (measured), then FlashingInvisTimer 0x68: the navi is not drawn on frames where the timer's bit 1 is set (2 hidden / 2 shown; blindVisualHandledHere_8016934).

Integration check in the normal fight (debug build): chip window, five picks, then A five times -- sword swing with its arc, sword held, heal streaks, presentation chips holding the fight. All twelve matched chips run through the same code as the sterile comparisons.

Backgrounds-on comparison, step 1: the field's halves were the opposite colours to the real ROM's (the player's half is the red one). Whole-screen difference 99.2% -> 59.4%; the field region now differs only by the two actors (the real capture is mid-cannon, ours idle) and a bottom strip. The backdrop layer is still missing.

Idle-vs-idle with backgrounds on (real enemy HP poked to match): the field region is now 92.6% identical -- the only difference there is the Mettaur's pose. What remains is the backdrop layer, the HUD (HP box, emotion window, CUSTOM gauge) and the chip-name strip at the bottom.

The battle backdrop, rendered from the real ROM's BG1 VRAM: a 32x32-tile map of the teal-arc motif on navy, palette bank 0. It scrolls 1 px left every 2 frames and 1 px up every 4. Its tiles are dword_8617488 (data/dat38_60.s:49372, 138 tiles) -- though the ROM order is not the VRAM order, and the tilemap itself is not in any data blob, so the upload routine is next.
M-CANNON matched: tools/chip_compare.py 03 demo-mcannon -> 0 px on every frame. Same cannon pose and barrel as Cannon/HiCannon, with the barrel's palette 2 (byte_80B8BD4 row 2).

AREAGRAB: the field now tracks per-panel ownership. Each grab takes the enemy's front-most column a row at a time, skipping any panel someone stands on -- three grabs in this demo move the boundary from 3/3 to 5/1, with the Mettaur's own panel left as the enemy's. Movement bounds follow ownership, so the stolen columns open up for the player.

Vulcan2/Vulcan3's last differing frame, before the fix: real (top) still in the firing pose with recoil and muzzle flash, ours (middle) already in recovery. Measuring the firing pose's last frame (c21/c35/c46) and the gun's life (35/46/57) gave the per-volley timings that took both to zero.

The elemental swords before the fix: real (top), ours (middle), diff (bottom) for FireSwrd and ElecSwrd. The sword objects were already exact -- only the arc kept the default blue. The strike ORs (subfamily - 0xb) into the spawn as a palette offset, so the arc takes the element's colour; with that, all four diff to zero.

HP numbers: the player's HP is now a box at the top left, and every HP number lags the real value the way the game's does -- on a change the shown number walks by |difference|/8 + 2 a frame and flashes in one of the game's two alternate digit sets (sub_801C168/sub_801C1D0, asm00_2.s:25853). All three pre-coloured digit sets are exported now.

SUPRVULC matched: tools/chip_compare.py 08 demo-suprvulc --frames 113 -> 0 px on every frame of the attack. Ten shots, firing state 100 frames and the gun on screen 112, measured from the real ROM the way Vulcan2/3 were. (Comparing past the attack's end shows a false residual: the demo's auto-fire starts a second volley the real capture never fires.)

StepSwrd: real (top), ours (middle), diff (bottom) at c0, c4, c10, c16, c29. The navi and the slash are identical wherever they can be compared -- the differences are the deleted enemy dissolving beside the dashed navi and the screen-wide red flash of its DELETED sequence, both artifacts of the capture setup rather than the chip.

StepSwrd re-measured: the navi's body colour is on the enemy's front column for the attack's first 24 frames, so the dash is immediate. The 705px residual is an afterimage of the navi's idle silhouette left on the home panel, blinking 2 frames on 2 off from frame 1 to 18, which nothing draws on the Rust side; the real row also shows a pink warp ring as the navi returns at frame 24. The afterimage's red-only look under --disable-bg is an mGBA blend artifact for semi-transparent objects, not the game. The game refuses chip use after the deletion sequence, so a no-enemy save state is impossible; --clean-state removed and replaced by --hide-enemy, which keeps the enemy immortal and blanks its object tiles.

StepSwrd's afterimage implemented and verified: the navi's idle silhouette on the panel it stepped off, two frames on and two off, from the attack's frame 1 through 18. Frames 0-11 now match the real ROM at zero pixels, step and all five blinks included. The remaining differences are from frame 12 (the slash, ~200px) and frame 24 (the return: a pink warp ring the Rust side does not draw, and the recovery pose).

StepSwrd's afterimage is a real red palette, not a capture artifact. Found a harness bug first: --dump ran before the frame loop, so every dump pictured the save state instead of the frame being examined. Fixed, and re-reading OBJ palette RAM on the right frame shows the game loads a bank that is the navi's palette with green and blue zeroed. Implemented as a red-only palette mode; StepSwrd is now 164 px/frame over 40 frames with 20 frames at exactly 0, down from 340. What remains is a second afterimage on the panel the navi steps to, which blinks on its own schedule over a navi still drawn in normal colours.

BigBomb matched: its nine-panel blast is now pixel-exact on every frame across the whole screen. The puffs overlap, so the order they are drawn decides which seams show, and that order was the entire remaining difference. Read it straight out of the real ROM's object memory on a blast frame: the nine puffs sit in memory as centre, left, right of the front row, then centre, right, left of the middle row, then the same for the back row, with the lowest index on top.

StepSwrd's second afterimage: the panel the navi steps to carries a red copy that trails the navi by exactly three frames, refreshed on the first frame of each two-frame blink and held for the second. Read object by object out of the real ROM's object memory: the copy on frames 16 and 17 has precisely the sizes and positions the navi's four sprites had on frame 13. StepSwrd is now 79 px/frame over 40 frames, from 340 at the start; frames 0 to 19 are all zero apart from the standing one-frame banner artifact and a single stray pixel.

StepSwrd is down to 43 px/frame from 340, with 31 of its 40 frames pixel-exact. The last pieces: the afterimage copies the sword as well as the navi while the sword is still on the far panel, and the sword itself follows the navi home rather than staying where it spawned. What is left is one unavoidable banner artifact and a 954-pixel difference on frame 29 that has not been looked at.

Four new chips matched frame for frame: Barr100 and Barr200 (the same barrier chip with a bigger bubble in gold and pink), and EnergBom and MegEnBom (MiniBomb's family and throw on the same bomb sprite's other pair of animations, tumbling in flight). The bomb's sprite was identified without reading any disassembly, by pulling the real bomb's tiles out of video memory at a chosen frame and searching the sprite's graphics blobs for those exact bytes.

StepSwrd holds its recovery pose one frame longer than the other swords: the real navi is still in it on the attack's frame 29 and idle on 30, where Sword, WideSwrd and Muramasa are idle on 29. That takes frame 29's home panel from 886 pixels to 84 and the chip from 43 to 23 per frame, with 33 of its 40 frames exact. What is left is a sword copy the far panel keeps after the return, at 68 pixels a frame.

The field tile layer now matches the real ROM exactly, zero pixels different across the whole layer. It was short by one tilemap row: the real ROM draws a front lip below the bottom panel row, five tiles repeating per column in that column's own side palette, which is the six pixels the field was missing at the bottom. Its tiles were already in the exported tileset, so this added a tilemap row and no new art. Found by teaching the capture harness to leave exactly one background layer on.

The battle backdrop is implemented and matches the real ROM: all 1024 cells of its tilemap carry identical tile art and identical flip and palette bits, and it scrolls at the real rate, one pixel left every two frames and one pixel up every four. The hand-off doc had recorded that the tilemap is not in any ROM data blob and that the tile blob's order is not the order the game uploads. Matching every tile byte for byte against the blob resolved both: the map is stored as blob indices, so the exporter needs only the disassembly.

Tile parity with the sprites turned off, real ROM above and this build below. Both background layers now match: the field is pixel-identical and the backdrop's tilemap is identical in all 1024 cells, so the only difference across the field is the backdrop's scroll phase, which depends on when the battle started. What is left is the HUD layer the real ROM keeps on BG3: the HP box and CUSTOM gauge across the top, worth 5409 pixels, and the chip name along the bottom, worth 1224. Those hold live values, so they need a tile-based renderer rather than a static map.

The site's playable demos now render both background layers: the real ROM above, a demo ROM below. The backdrop scrolls behind the field at the game's own rate and the field carries its front lip, so the only thing still missing from the tiles is the HUD strip and the chip name, which the real ROM draws on its own layer. The enemy and HP number in the lower shot are the demo's own, not a mismatch.

The HP box is now drawn in tiles the way the real ROM draws it, real above and this build below. Each digit is two tiles stacked and the set steps by two per digit, so the box is a left cap, four slots filled right-aligned with a blank in the leading positions, and a right cap. The art is a fourth variant of the font the project already exports, found in the same file by scanning its symbols for the digit-zero tiles: all ten digits match the real ROM's, and the box frame follows in the same blob. The numbers differ only because the demo starts at 100 HP and the captured battle is at 60. The CUSTOM gauge beside it is still to do.

The CUSTOM gauge is now drawn in tiles, real ROM above and this build below. Its art is in the same data file as the HP font, loaded at a fixed video tile so the mapping is a constant offset. The layout is one label row of white CUSTOM text on a dark filler, and one bar row of an end cap, six body cells, the four-cell L-or-R marker, six more body cells and a mirrored cap. The marker is cyan while the gauge fills and orange once it is full, which is the swap the gauge shows instead of any proportional readout. The remaining difference in this pair is live state, not art: the demo is at 80 HP with a part-filled gauge, the captured battle at 60 with a full one. The HUD strip is down from 5409 pixels to 812.

The chip select screen, real ROM above and this build below, after correcting its palette banks. My asset had two palettes swapped relative to the real ROM: the window's frame belongs in bank 9 and the panel behind it in bank 13, and this build was putting the panel's palette into the frame's bank, which is why the whole window rendered salmon where the real one is grey. With that fixed the header, the CHIP SELECT label, the OK button and the icon row all land. Still to do: the preview card's name and its code and damage row, the vertical meter, and the strip below the icons.

The chip select screen after three more fixes, real ROM above and this build below. The field slides fifteen pixels down out of the window's way when the menu opens, at one and a half pixels a frame over ten frames, which the real ROM does and this build did not. The HP box is not hidden by the menu: the real ROM redraws it fifteen tile columns over, beside the window and above the field, so it does that now too. And the icon slots were taking one palette bank each, running over the bank the HP box shares with the window's panel, which painted the box in a chip's colours. The right half of the screen goes from 15443 differing pixels to 6618. Still off: the preview card's name and its code and damage row, the vertical meter, and the strip below the icons.

The chip select window, real ROM left and this build right, after finding the palette its icons actually use. The real ROM draws every chip icon and the vertical meter from a single shared bank, and that bank is a greyscale ramp, so its icons are grey on pale yellow rather than each chip's own colours. This build was giving every slot its own bank and its chip's palette, which is why the meter came out yellow and checkered. The shared palette is in neither the window data nor the chip data, so it is now read off a live menu and carried in the asset. The window area drops from 10321 differing pixels to 8151. What is left is mostly the preview card's name and its code and damage row, which the game composes at runtime with a proportional font.

The chip select window, real ROM above and this build below. The window has ten slot cells in two rows of five, and only five chips are offered here; the real ROM draws its empty icon in every cell it is not offering, while this build drew only the five it had, leaving the lower row transparent so the battle field showed through the window. Filling them takes the window area from 8151 differing pixels to 6999. Still open: the two frame columns flanking the pick stack, where the real ROM alternates two tiles down the column in the shared icon bank and this build has a single tile in the window bank.

The chip select window, real ROM above and this build below, with the pick stack's frame now drawn. Its two columns are not in the window's stored map, because the game patches those cells in when the window opens, and their tiles are not in the window's own tile block either: they are the first two tiles of a separate block the game uploads elsewhere in video memory. They alternate down both columns in the window's own bank. Three things had to line up: exporting the tiles, stopping the slide-in from repainting those cells from the stored map, and using the right bank. The window area is down to 6319 differing pixels from 10321 when I started on it.

The preview card, real ROM left and this build right. The card's name row and its element, code and damage row are composed at runtime from a proportional font, so this build cannot draw them yet; it was leaving those cells transparent, which let the scrolling backdrop show straight through the card. They are now filled with the card's own dark interior tile, which is what the real ROM puts in the parts of those rows it is not writing text into. The window area drops to 5012 differing pixels, from 10321 when I started on the chip select screen. The picture itself already matched.

The battle text font is solved and drawing. The real ROM writes a chip's name along the bottom from a font of two-tile glyphs, one glyph per label in the ROM data, and the glyph index turns out to be the game's own character code, so the disassembly's character map indexes the font directly. Reading it from one label earlier than I first found makes code 0x0d render as C, 0x26 as a and 0x33 as n, exactly as the map says. This shot is the renderer drawing through that font in the right place and palette. What is left is the trigger: the name should appear while a chip is in use, and the demo that has the HUD does not fire one.

The chip name strip, real ROM above and this build below. The name is drawn from the game's own text font, whose glyph index is its character code, and the damage figure follows it in the second, orange digit set carried in the HUD asset. The trigger was backwards at first: the real ROM names the chip that is ABOUT to be used, not the one in flight. Measured on a capture where the name stands from the first frame and clears on the frame the chip fires, so it follows the front of the hand. The two strips differ only in which chip each build is holding.

Battle tile parity, real ROM above and this build below, sprites off so only the tilemaps show. Every layer is now drawn: the backdrop scrolling behind, the field with its front lip, the HP box, the CUSTOM gauge with its label and marker, and the chip name with its damage figure. Nothing structural is missing. What still differs is live state rather than art: the captured battle is at 60 HP with a full gauge holding a Cannon, this build at 100 with an empty gauge holding a HiCannon, and the backdrop sits at a different scroll phase because the two battles started at different times. The whole screen is down from 10134 differing pixels to 7523, and the field alone is within 147.

LilBolr1 captured from the real ROM, the next chip family to build. The navi throws, a gold ball arcs off the top of the frame with damage numbers popping, and a white spray then opens on the panels ahead. The throw is machinery this build already has; the spray is new. Its sprite is identified as sprite_8399578, which took all three searches to find: it is in none of the plain sprite files and none of the compressed ones, and only turned up in the assembled data blobs.

LilBolr in flight, real ROM above and this build below. What it lobs is the LilBoiler virus, a golden kettle, not a bomb, and it now draws from that virus's own sprite. Its arc is far taller than a bomb's: the ball rises about a hundred pixels above the panel, peaking eleven frames in and landing on the same fortieth frame a bomb does, which needs both a faster launch and a stronger pull. The chip is down from around a thousand differing pixels a frame to 390. Left: the kettle sits about thirteen pixels high, the flame on its lid is missing, and the damage figure that pops beneath it is a separate feature. Its blast already matches, because it is the same blast object MiniBomb uses.

LilBolr1, 2 and 3 at the same frame, whose chip powers are 100, 140 and 180. All three show the same figure of 40 under the thing they throw, so that figure is not the chip's damage. Taken with the thrown object being a virus sprite, it is the summoned LilBoiler's own HP, which makes this chip a summon rather than a throw. One capture of the three settled a question that reasoning about the chip data could not.

The chip name was drawing over the chip select window's bottom edge. The real ROM shows no name there while the menu is up, because the window covers that strip; this build kept writing it, so HiCannon40 sat across the window's lower frame. Hiding it with the menu open takes that strip from 497 differing pixels to 64 and the window to 5012. The lower half of this shot is the pick stack, real left and mine right, which matches.

The chip select window's pick stack, real ROM left and this build right, now identical to the pixel. Its two frame columns are the same pair of tiles, but the right column is the left one mirrored, which the real ROM's map does with a flip bit. Drawing both unmirrored left one tile column wrong down the whole stack: the same pixels in the same colours, just facing the wrong way, which is why the colour counts on the two sides matched exactly while 600 pixels differed. That was the hint worth following.

FlshBom's held ball, real ROM left and this build right, at both of its positions. The ball is raised partway through the throw, and unlike MiniBomb the sprite does not encode that: every frame of it carries the same part offsets, so the game moves the object itself. Measured, it sits at one spot through the attack's frame 4 and another from frame 5. With that and the sprite's own part offsets, the whole held phase is within 51 pixels a frame and the chip is at 102, from unimplemented.

HUD parity, real ROM above and this build below. The HP box's right cap is the left one mirrored, the same flip bit the pick stack's frame needed, and setting it takes the box from 149 differing pixels to 33. What is left across the whole HUD is live state and backdrop scroll phase, not art: the box's 33 is 60 against 100, the gauge's 880 is an empty bar against a full one with its marker cyan rather than orange, and the label row's 91 is backdrop showing through the gaps at a different scroll phase. The gauge's own caps are within 2 pixels.

Per-pixel tile parity for the whole battle screen: zero differing pixels out of 38400, real ROM above and this build below with sprites off. Getting a true number needed a fixture that matches the captured battle's state, 60 HP with a full gauge and a Cannon in hand, so that a difference means art rather than state. Building it exposed a real bug that the state mismatch had been hiding: the chip name was read by indexing the chip table with the chip's id, but the table is in the exporter's own order, so every name was the wrong chip. Taking the name from the chip in hand fixes it, and every layer then reads zero: HUD, backdrop, field and name strip.

FlshBom1-3 reach per-pixel parity. The thrown ball was still using the MiniBomb sprite, its arc was a bomb's, and the held ball dragged a ground shadow the real ROM does not draw. With its own launch speed and gravity -- solved against the ball tracked frame by frame by its four yellow colours over the whole forty-frame flight -- and the held shadow suppressed, every frame of the attack now differs by 0 pixels from the real ROM. Real on top, this build in the middle, the difference below; the band above the line is the HUD, which the sterile arena does not reproduce.
FlshBom in motion: the real ROM on the left, this build on the right, half speed. The whole throw -- the ball raised on frame 5, the forty-frame arc, the recovery -- is identical pixel for pixel.
Sword, real ROM left and this build right at half speed: the pose, the arc object spawned at the navi's front and the five frames of recovery. 0 px on every frame.

BigBomb, real left and this build right. The nine blast puffs overlap, so the order they are pushed decides which seams show; they are pushed back to front in the order the real ROM's OAM has them. 0 px on every frame.

Barrier, real left and this build right. The bubble's palette bank is the one the sterile arena would otherwise hand to the backdrop, which is why the backdrop's bank is assigned only in a full battle.

The chip select window, real ROM left and this build middle, sprites turned off on both so only the tile layers are compared. The window frame, the pick stack and its frame, the OK box, the CHIP SELECT panel and the code row are identical. What is left is the card picture and the icons, which are different chips because the two folders differ, and one real defect: the real ROM draws EIGHT slot cells and this build draws ten. Cells nine and ten are written in the frame's palette bank there, which makes them read as the panel's own background rather than as empty cells -- the white block at the bottom right of the difference.

The battle HUD reaches per-pixel parity. Rows one and two are the real ROM and this build with everything on; rows three and four are the HUD layer alone on each side; row five is their difference, which is empty -- 0 px of the whole strip. Three fixes got there. The EMOTION WINDOW, the navi's face under the HP box, was missing: the real ROM draws it as two OBJECTS rather than tiles, which is why it survives the field being stripped, and its art turned up at dword_872D814 by searching the disassembly for the twelve tiles taken out of OBJ VRAM. The player's HP was being drawn TWICE, once in the tile box and once in object text under it, so the object one is gone. And a FULL CUSTOM GAUGE FLOWS: its body cell steps through four patterns seven frames each and the L-or-R marker alternates cyan and orange every eight, which is a tilemap swap -- the tile art and the palette bank never change.

The CHIP SELECT panel, real ROM left and this build middle, sprites off, difference right. This build drew ten slot cells where the real ROM shows eight. The count is fixed, not a function of how many chips are offered: sub_8027E90 copies a template into the twelve per-slot records whose low bytes give cells 1-8 one state and cells 9-10 another, and the palette pass maps the second to the window frame's bank -- where the game writes flat background, not the empty-cell art. Everything left in the difference is the two builds holding different chips.

Chip select with sprites on: real ROM left, this build right. Two objects were missing or wrong. The gold ring above the pick stack -- the regular-chip mark, and a red disc with a slash when no regular chip is set -- was not drawn at all; the real ROM hangs it in a 32x32 OAM entry at (87,-4) whose only four non-blank tiles are the ring, and those four turned up at byte_86F5834 by searching the disassembly for their bytes. It now matches pixel for pixel. And the cursor bracket was yellow where the real ROM's is orange: the window's stored cursor palette is its BACKGROUND bank word for word, and the bracket sprites draw from the OBJECT bank instead. What is left is the two builds holding different chips.

LilBolr1-3: 333.6 px/frame down to 34.6. Real ROM on top, this build in the middle, the difference below. The chip lobs the LilBoiler VIRUS, not a bomb, and the figure riding under it is the summoned boiler's own HP -- it reads 40 for all three variants, whose powers are 100, 140 and 180 -- so it is a constant, not the chip's damage. That figure also turned up the fact that this build's HP digits were drawn in a made-up palette: flat white on black where the game's is a soft white with a dark blue outline. The real one is dword_86B7AC0, the 32 bytes immediately before the battle text font, and dumping OBJ bank 14 out of a live battle gives it back word for word. What is left is a one-pixel wobble on six frames of forty-eight.

The battle backdrop ANIMATES, which this build had missed. Top row is the real ROM's backdrop layer at three moments, bottom row is this build's: the little magenta digits inside the rings fade in and out. It is the TILE ART that cycles -- seven complete sets of the layer's 37 tiles, eight frames each, a 56-frame loop -- while the map's 1024 entries, the palette bank and the scroll all stand still. Dumping BG1's char data frame by frame is what shows it; dumping the map or the palette shows nothing at all. All 259 tiles were matched byte for byte against the disassembly's blob, so the exporter still needs only the submodule. A still backdrop differs from the real ROM by about 280 px a frame; with the animation the best alignment found is 150. The rest is phase: the game's horizontal and vertical scroll phases are independent, and this build ties them to one counter, so most of the 64x64 phase lattice is unreachable and the two rings' grids sit at different offsets above.

Whole-screen tile parity, restored with the animation in: real ROM left, this build middle, difference right -- 0 px of 38400, every background layer, sprites off. Getting here needed a longer capture than before. The backdrop's art loop is 56 frames and its scroll repeats every 128, so the two only line up every 896; add the CUSTOM gauge's own 112-frame flow and a matching frame is rare. The earlier measurement searched a hundred frames and found nothing, which read as a regression and was not one. Two other things had to be fixed to measure it at all: the RGB555-to-8-bit expansion in the analysis script was v*255/31 where the emulator uses v<<3|v>>2, which put a one-off on most pixels and made every exact match fail; and the HUD fixture held a full gauge, which opened the chip window that the demo -- pressing nothing -- could never close, so a long capture had no battle screen in it.

The chip select window is at per-pixel parity: real ROM left, this build middle, difference right -- 0 px, sprites and all. The way in was identifying the capture's own chips: each slot's four icon tiles were pulled out of VRAM and matched against every one of the 411 chips' icons in byte_8725894, which named them Vulcan1 D, AirShot *, Sword S, MiniBomb B and Cannon A -- and the pick stack's icon is that Cannon, so the fifth slot is not empty, it is picked. demo-custmatch offers exactly those five with the Cannon picked and the cursor on OK. Four defects fell out. A picked slot keeps its CODE and loses only its icon. A slot's code comes from the FOLDER ENTRY, not the chip's first code, so a folder's copies letter differently. The card shows a 'sending chip data' message whenever the cursor is not on a previewable chip, and that message is a static 7x6 image at dword_87225B4. And the pick stack's frame is four tiles, not two: its top two rows have their own pair.

The chip in hand hangs over the navi, and this build was not drawing it. Real ROM left, this build right -- the navi stands a column further along in the fixture, which is why the two icons are forty pixels apart, but the height matches to the pixel. It is a 16x16 object whose four tiles are the chip's own icon, the same art the chip window's slots use, at its panel's centre one left and fifty-six up; only its OBJECT palette was new, byte_872CFD4, which is not the window's icon bank and differs from it at two entries. It is deliberately left out of the sterile arena: the object belongs to the chip window closing rather than to the hand's contents, and the real captures poke a chip straight into the hand slot and show none.

The chip scoreboard, every comparison run in one pass: 36 of 38 exact. Each row is a chip's mean pixels per frame against its FLOOR -- the mean the ENEMY DELETED banner's single unmovable frame alone puts on a run of that length, 369 divided by the frame count -- so a chip is exact when its mean equals its floor. Running them all together immediately caught something a chip-at-a-time check had missed: the chip-in-hand icon's palette was being allocated for every battle, including the sterile arena that never draws it, and SuprVulc -- the longest volley in the game -- then ran out of object palette banks and crashed. It reads its floor now. The two that are not exact are BlkBomb, over by 2.2 a frame, and LilBolr by 26.9, both a one-pixel wobble on a handful of frames.

The RESULT window, real ROM left and this build middle: it had never been compared, because the demo needs a chip press the capture harness cannot land. demo-resultmatch puts it up at once with the capture's own readout -- 0:29:33 is 1760 frames, busting level 2 -- and three things came out of it. The window RESTED IN THE WRONG PLACE: 24 px right and 16 px down of where this build had it, which is three tile columns and two tile rows, so the disassembly's 'rests at x = 3' is a tile column and not a pixel. ITS PALETTES WERE THE GAUGE'S: the window draws in banks 9 to 11 and the CUSTOM gauge holds bank 9 all fight, so it came up in the gauge's greens and yellows until the banks were taken back on open. And the REWARD PICTURE was missing -- the coin in the GET DATA box is a 7x6 image, the same shape as a chip card's, at dword_8732E54 with its own palette bank. The window box is down to 553 px, all of it the '100 z' reward text, which is composed at runtime from a proportional font this build does not have yet -- the same thing that blocks the chip card's name.

The whole battle screen, sprites and all: real ROM left, this build middle, difference right. Everything that is art lines up -- the animated backdrop, the field and its lip, the HP box, the CUSTOM gauge, the emotion window, the chip name strip, the chip-in-hand icon, the navi's pose and the Mettaur on the same panel in the same pose. The 1991 px that remain are live state and nothing else: this build's navi is at 40 HP where the capture's is at 60, its Mettaur carries the demo's padded HP so a chip can be fired at it repeatedly, a hit spark is in the air, and the gauge's flow animation is a few frames out of phase. Finding a frame to compare at all took a 1200-frame capture: the backdrop's art loop is 56 frames and its scroll repeats every 128, so they coincide only every 896.

PoisSeed, a new chip: real ROM on top, this build in the middle, the difference below -- 10.1 px/frame against a floor of 7.7, so 2.4 of real difference on six frames of forty-eight. The pod is byte_82F569C.spr, found by pulling the four tiles of its flying object out of OBJ VRAM and searching all 97 sprite files; animation 8 is the pod in the hand and 9 the pod in flight, matched by their OAM shapes against the real ROM's. Its magenta is palette 12 of the sprite's own block, which carries one palette per seed -- index 0 is IceSeed's blue -- reached as the chip's shift of 3, its attack_param_2, plus the OAM offset of 9 every part carries. Getting that colour out needed a bug fixed: the per-offset palettes were cached by the OAM offset alone, so a sprite whose first frame already carries an offset kept the palette it was built with however it was later shifted. Its arc needed no fitting at all -- the plain bomb launch and gravity put the pod on the real ROM's pixel at every frame of the flight.

PoisSeed, whole attack: real ROM on top, this build in the middle, the difference below -- 6.9 px/frame over seventy frames against a floor of 5.3. The throw, the arc, the landing and the POISON going down all match. The sheet is nine pairs of 32x32 objects, one pair per panel of the enemy's half because a panel is forty wide, all from byte_830E44C.spr; it grows from an ellipse to a full green sheet and then fades, leaving the panels poison underneath. Its timing took two measurements to place: spawned the moment the pod lands it runs a frame early, spawned a frame later it runs a frame late -- it is spawned a frame later AND already one tick in, so its first frame shows for exactly one frame. What is left is a shadow under the pod for six frames just after the throw.

All three seeds, this build: IceSeed, GrasSeed and PoisSeed. Two of them are EXACT against the real ROM over seventy frames and PoisSeed is 1.6 px/frame over its floor. They are one chip's worth of work between them -- the same pod sprite and the same nine-panel sheet, told apart by palette. The POD's palette is the chip's attack_param_2 as a shift on top of the OAM offset of 9 that every part carries: IceSeed 1, GrasSeed 2, PoisSeed 3, landing on the sprite's palettes 10, 11 and 12. The SHEET's does not follow it: PoisSeed and IceSeed share the sheet sprite's own palette 0 while GrasSeed takes 8, matched by dumping OBJ bank 1 while each sheet is up. Their panels are left alone in the sterile arena, where the real capture's field layer is stripped and cannot show them.

BugBomb and VDoll, the last two chips of the bomb family. Real ROM above this build in each pair. Both THROW AND STAY -- the object stops where it lands and keeps standing there, so neither bursts. BugBomb's ball is the seeds' own sprite in another animation and flies flatter and slower than a bomb; VDoll's doll is its own sprite, byte_83262C0, and arcs to the top of the screen and hangs there, needing its own launch, gravity and a sixty-frame flight. VDoll's HELD object is not the doll at all: it is the seeds' sprite again, animation 0, whose 16x16 part sits thirty left and twenty-eight up of the panel centre, exactly where the real ROM's OAM puts it. BugBomb is 35.4 px/frame against a floor of 5.3 and VDoll 10.7. With these the bomb family is complete: eleven chips.

The RESULT window's reward line, drawn at last: real ROM left, this build middle, difference right -- 80 px of the window's interior, all of it one row of the box's bottom border. The text was never proportional. It is the SAME fixed 8x16 font the chip name strip already uses, dword_86B7AE0, and the reason a live screen's tiles matched nothing in the ROM is that the game's text renderer does not copy glyphs unchanged: its loop adds a 32-bit colour word to every glyph word on the way to VRAM, and this window passes the index whose word is 0x88888888. The capture's '1' and '0' are glyphs 2 and 1 with 8 added to every nibble, byte for byte. The symbol after the amount is not a letter either -- it is glyph 0xb3 of the same font, found by searching all 448 of them. That also unblocks the chip card's name, which the same renderer draws the same way.

The chip card's NAME, real ROM left and this build middle, difference right. The name was the last thing on the card left blank, on the theory that it came from a proportional renderer this build does not have; it does not. It is the fixed 8x16 battle font, eight cells of it, with 8 added to every nibble on the way to VRAM -- the same colour add the RESULT window's reward line uses, from the same routine (sub_3006C18). The glyph index is the game's own character code, so constants/bn6-charmap.tbl indexes the font directly. Seeing the name at all needs a new fixture: with the cursor on OK the real ROM shows its 'sending chip data' card instead, so demo-cardname walks the cursor onto the first slot, and the real capture presses Left for six frames to do the same. The name row is now exact; the 183 pixels left are the code letter, the element icon and the damage, which are a different, bolder font that is not in the ROM uncompressed.

The whole preview card, real ROM left and this build right, four of the window's five chips: 0 differing pixels each, and the fifth (MiniBomb) too. The card's other three rows are not the battle font at all -- they are three little fonts of the window's own, stored ready-coloured so nothing is added on the way to VRAM: 28 code letters at dword_86E2E98 (A-Z, then '*' and a blank), ten damage digits at dword_86E411C, and eleven 16x16 element icons at dword_86E3598 indexed by the chip's element byte. None of them can be found by searching the ROM for the bytes a live screen shows, because every glyph begins with three blank rows and a tile-aligned search never lines up; searching for the SHAPE instead -- any one ink over any one background, starting at the first non-blank row -- found all three at once. The last thing wrong was colour: AirShot's wind icon came out black where the real one is white. The six words that follow the element icons are one row per element, and they are palette entries 10 to 15 of the shared icon bank -- 13 to 15 are the element's OWN colours, which the game writes as it draws the card. Reading that bank off a live menu had given zeros there because the menu happened to be showing a null-element chip, whose three are zero.

The RESULT window and the HUD above it, real ROM top, this build middle, difference bottom -- 0 differing pixels across the window, its badge and the HP box. Four things closed the last of it. The GET DATA readout's bottom edge: the window's stored map has a tile there whose top pixel row is lit, and the live window's ten cells are flat, so the game replaces that run as it draws the reward -- 80 pixels, one pixel row. The CUSTOM gauge: the real ROM drops the whole thing, label, bar and caps, the moment the results come up, and keeps only the HP box. The emotion window goes with it. And the badge at the window's top-left corner is not part of the window at all: it is the chip select screen's regular-chip mark, hung as OAM entry 0, a 16x16 at (37,21) in object bank 11 -- the same art and the same bank, byte for byte. Everything still red is the field and backdrop outside the window, which the fixture does not reproduce: a different enemy, a different backdrop phase.

The two worst arcs in the scoreboard, fixed by sweeping rather than fitting. Each pair is real ROM above, this build below: LilBolr's boiler at the four frames that used to differ most (430, 358, 251 and 165 pixels), then BugBomb's ball at its four. All eight are 0 now. The sweep put both chips on BlkBomb's own across-speed, and BugBomb on BlkBomb's gravity as well, so the thrown things share a launcher and differ mostly in how hard it throws -- start a new chip's arc from those two constants and sweep the launch speed alone. Sweeping needs care in one respect: the launch speed and the gravity trade off along a ridge, because a taller throw with a harder pull looks the same, so step ALONG the ridge and not across it, and every minimum found here was a plateau several hundred wide. LilBolr goes from 26.9 pixels a frame over its floor to 1.4, BugBomb from 30.1 to 1.1, VDoll from 5.4 to 2.0. What is left in each is no longer the arc: tracking the object's bounding box frame by frame shows the paths now agreeing exactly, and the residue is one frame before a landing, a boiler's flame a step out of phase, and a ground shadow that starts larger than this build draws it and settles over six frames. The emotion window is gone from the sterile arena too, which the real ROM drops with the last enemy.
